Rolls-Royce Ghost Shooting Brake Wants To Redefine the Luxury Family Car – Rendering
8 photos
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik
Has Rolls-Royce expanded its lineup with a veritable family-oriented cruiser as a low-riding alternative to the Cullinan? After all, that’s what a five-door version of its Ghost luxury sedan would be.
The answer is obviously no. As we said in the title, this is a mere rendering of such a project, and before delving into some of the things that define it, we have to mention the obvious. And that’s the fact that something like this will never happen.
First and foremost, it would be a niche car, with no direct competitors. After all, it’s not like Mercedes-Maybach and Bentley want to add station wagon versions of their S-Class and Flying Spur, respectively. Second, estates are not exactly popular anymore, with crossovers and SUVs stealing their thunder, so Rolls-Royce will definitely not risk injecting a huge amount of money into something that might not sell in sufficient numbers to justify the investment.
With this information off our chest, let’s move on to the actual car itself, which was sketched out by @kelsonik and shared on his social media a few days ago. The rendered Rolls-Royce Ghost Shooting Brake features the same front fascia as the sedan. In fact, it is pretty much identical up to the B-pillars. Further back, it has a much longer roofline, as well as bigger rear three-quarter windows, and redesigned rear three-quarter panels.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik The magic happens at the end, where it features a tailgate that opens up into a huge cargo area, instead of a traditional trunk lid. The taillights are identical, and so is the rear bumper. The tailpipes carry over from the real thing, and so does pretty much everything else. We can see that the fuel filler cap is still positioned on the right rear three-quarter panel, and that this thing features a green paint finish, some black elements, and rides on entirely new wheels that are much larger than the standard ones.
Based on the facelifted iteration of the Rolls-Royce Ghost, namely the Series II, this virtual project also features the same interior, although it is not visible in these digital illustrations. This means the same three separate displays behind the full-width glass panel, as well as the Spirit operating system, choreographed interior illumination sequence, and almost countless personalization options and high-end features, among other things.
Power would also be supplied by the familiar V12 engine, which is a twin-turbocharged unit, in case you forgot. The mill has a 6.75-liter displacement, and develops 563 hp (571 ps/420 kW) and 627 pound-feet (850 Nm) of torque. The Rolls-Royce Ghost takes 4.6 seconds to reach 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill, and 4.8 seconds from 0-62 mph (0-100 kph). As for its top speed, it is electronically limited to 155 mph (250 kph).
Those who want more goodies from their Rolls-Royce Ghost can get the superior Black Badge. It features a few updates inside and out, comes with 22-inch forged wheels, and offers more oomph. The output is now officially rated at 592 hp (600 ps/441 kW) and the peak thrust stands at 664 pound-feet (900 Nm). However, that does not make it faster, because the company quoted the same 4.6 seconds from 0-60 mph as in the regular version of the luxury sedan.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik Even though it competes against the likes of the Bentley Flying Spur and the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class, the Rolls-Royce Ghost is a lot more expensive than its main rivals in the class. For the 2027 model year, you are looking at a minimum of $375,000 for one of these, and it can easily exceed $425,000. Some versions of the car can cost half a million dollars. The Flying Spur starts from over $250,000, and the Maybach S-Class is available from more than $210,000.
Some say that the Ghost is the absolute best-of-the-best in its class, arguing that the S-Class and the Flying Spur do not come anywhere near it. Others would agree to disagree, and they’d pick the Mercedes-Maybach or the Bentley over the Rolls-Royce all day, any day. But if there is one Rolls-Royce that has no direct rivals, it is the Phantom. This gargantuan sedan sits in a league of its own, measuring up to 235.5 inches (5,981 mm) in length for the EWB (Extended Wheelbase), which has 184.5 inches (3,772 mm) between the axles.
As you likely recall, all vehicles currently made by Rolls-Royce utilize the same construction. The platform is called the Architecture of Luxury, and it is the foundation stone not only of the Ghost and Phantom luxury sedans, but also the Cullinan luxury SUV, and the Spectre luxury electric grand tourer. And no, no Bimmers are based on this platform.
Now, assuming that Rolls-Royce would indeed go ahead and green light the Ghost Shooting Brake , would you spend your money on a station wagon version of the British luxury sedan? That’s a tough question to answer, but for what it’s worth, I definitely like the design as sketched out by the quoted pixel master. Do you?
